newsitem.title: USA: USDA boosts wheat forecast, but not corn, soybeans.
newsitem.headline: USDA boosts wheat forecast, but not corn, soybeans.

text.p: Near-perfect growing conditions in the Southern Plains in May set the stage for U.S. farmers to harvest 2.30 billion bushels of wheat in 1997, up 43 million from initial expectations and the largest crop in threee years, the Agriculture Department said on Thursday.
But the department left its forecast of 1997 corn production unchanged at 9.84 billion bushels, despite cool Midwestern weather that many analysts expect to trim yields.

The department pegged the 1997 U.S. winter wheat crop-- which makes up about 70 percent of the total U.S. wheat crop-- at 1.60 billion bushels, up 3 percent from its May estimate and 8 percent from 1996 production.

Most analysts had expected such a move because of good weather in May that helped recoup some losses that occurred when a hard freeze hit the winter wheat crop in Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas and Colorado in April.

The department also forecast the U.S. soybean crop at a record 2.60 billion bushels, unchanged from last month. But soybeans should continue to be in short supply until the fall harvest, it said. The department raised its estimate of pre-harvest soybeans stocks only slightly to 130 million bushels, from 125 million in May, due to increased imports, which have angered some farmers.

The department went out on a limb in May and forecast average U.S. corn yields at 131 bushels per acre, or 3 bushels higher than the normal year-to-year "trend" increase would suggest. The department keep its forecast unchanged on Thursday, despite cool Midwestern weather that many analysts think will reduce yields.
